section.title: Rebuilding the Altar and Foundation
section.sectionRationale: Before a single wall of the temple rises, the returned remnant rebuilds the altar and restores the sacrifices, keeps the appointed feasts, and then lays the foundation with worship. The chapter shows a people whose first instinct is to draw near to God in the way He commanded, and it ends with the strange, mingled sound of joy and weeping at what has begun.
section.thesis: The restoration of God's people begins at the altar, with obedient worship offered in fear yet in faith, so that when the foundation is laid the community responds with a mixture of soaring joy and grief that only a greater temple could finally answer.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the altar rebuilt and the sacrifices and feasts restored, verses 1 to 6; preparations and the laying of the foundation, verses 7 to 10; and the great sound of joy and weeping, verses 11 to 13.

units.label: The altar rebuilt and worship restored
units.note: as it is written in the Law of Moses

verses.text: By the seventh month, the Israelites had settled in their towns, and the people assembled as one man in Jerusalem.

Then Jeshua son of Jozadak and his fellow priests, along with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his associates, began to build the {{mizbeach|altar}} of the God of Israel to sacrifice burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the {{torah|Law of Moses}} the man of God.
They set up the altar on its foundation and sacrificed {{olah|burnt offerings}} on it to the LORD, both the morning and evening burnt offerings, even though they feared the people of the land.
They also celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles in accordance with what is written, and they offered burnt offerings daily based on the number prescribed for each day.
After that, they presented the regular burnt offerings and those for New Moons and for all the appointed sacred feasts of the LORD, as well as all the freewill offerings brought to the LORD.
On the first day of the seventh month, the Israelites began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid.

units.label: The foundation of the temple laid
units.note: cedar from Lebanon, and Levites to supervise

verses.text: They gave money to the masons and carpenters, and food and drink and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring cedar logs from Lebanon to Joppa by sea, as authorized by Cyrus king of Persia.

In the second month of the second year after they had arrived at the house of God in Jerusalem, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Jeshua son of Jozadak, and the rest of their associates including the priests, the Levites, and all who had returned to Jerusalem from the captivity, began the work. They appointed Levites twenty years of age or older to supervise the construction of the house of the LORD.

So Jeshua and his sons and brothers, Kadmiel and his sons (descendants of Yehudah), and the sons of Henadad and their sons and brothers, all Levites, joined together to supervise those working on the house of God.

units.label: Joy and weeping at the foundation
units.note: the people could not distinguish the shouts from the weeping

verses.text: When the builders had laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their apparel with trumpets, and the Levites (the sons of Asaph) with cymbals, took their positions to praise the LORD, as David king of Israel had prescribed.

And they sang responsively with praise and thanksgiving to the LORD: “For He is good; for His {{chesed|loving devotion}} to Israel endures forever.” Then all the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid.
But many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple. Still, many others shouted joyfully.
The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people were making so much noise. And the sound was heard from afar.

mizbeach.gloss: Altar, literally a place of sacrifice, from the verb to slaughter. The remnant builds the altar first, before the temple itself, because atoning worship is the foundation of their life with God. Every altar in Israel points forward to the cross, where the true and final sacrifice is offered.

torah.gloss: The Law, or instruction, of Moses. The people do not improvise their worship; they act as it is written. The recurring phrase in accordance with what is written shows a community determined to obey God's revealed word, the pattern the whole book commends.

olah.gloss: The burnt offering, literally that which goes up, wholly consumed on the altar and ascending as smoke to God. It expressed total dedication and atonement. Its complete surrender foreshadows Christ, who offered Himself wholly to God for us.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast covenant love, loyalty, and mercy. The refrain sung at the foundation, His loving devotion to Israel endures forever, is Israel's great confession of God's faithful love, the same love that carries His people through exile and home again, and that meets us fully in Christ.

basic.context: Once settled in their towns, the returned exiles gather in Jerusalem in the seventh month and, before building the temple, they rebuild the altar and start the sacrifices again, keeping the Feast of Tabernacles exactly as the Law commands. They do this even though they are afraid of the hostile peoples around them. Then they lay the temple's foundation with a service of praise, and the crowd erupts in a sound that is joy and weeping at once. The question is: where does true restoration begin? At the altar, with God.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative history, showing us a good example rather than issuing commands. The repeated phrase as it is written signals the point: worship should follow God's word, not our preferences. We should not copy the animal sacrifices, which are fulfilled in Christ, but we should copy the priority the people gave to worshiping God rightly, promptly, and together, even under pressure.
basic.originalLanguages: The first thing rebuilt is the mizbeach, the altar, the place of sacrifice. They offer the olah, the burnt offering that goes up wholly to God, and they do it according to the torah, the Law of Moses. At the foundation they sing the great refrain of God's chesed, His steadfast covenant love that endures forever.
basic.typology: The altar and burnt offerings point to the cross, where Christ is the true sacrifice offered wholly to God. The temple foundation points to Christ the cornerstone, on whom God's true house is built.
basic.christ: The people put the altar first because they knew they could not come to God without atonement. That instinct is answered forever in Jesus, the once-for-all sacrifice, our true altar and Lamb. The mingled joy and weeping over a lesser temple looks ahead to the promise that God would fill His house with greater glory, a promise kept when Jesus, greater than the temple, walked into it.
basic.god: God is worthy of obedient, ordered worship, and He is faithful: the very refrain the people sing celebrates His covenant love that never ends. He receives the worship of a fearful, weak remnant and is pleased to dwell among them again.
basic.crossReferences: Haggai 2:3-9 addresses the disappointment over the smaller temple and promises greater glory. Hebrews 10 shows the burnt offerings fulfilled in Christ's one sacrifice. And 1 Corinthians 3:11 names Christ as the only foundation.
basic.oneStory: Restoration begins at the altar, because fellowship with God always rests on sacrifice. The remnant's obedient worship, and the tears over a temple that could not match the old, set us longing for the greater temple and the final sacrifice, both of which arrive in Jesus.

context.literary: Ezra 3 unfolds in three movements bound together by a single calendar note: the seventh month, mentioned in verse 1 and again in verse 6, frames the first movement like a pair of bookends and marks the high point of Israel's sacred year, when the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles cluster together within a few weeks. The narrator delays the founding of the temple itself until the second movement, verses 7 to 10, so that liturgically the altar and its sacrifices are already months old before a single foundation stone is laid, a sequence that echoes 1 Kings 5 to 8, where Solomon likewise gathered materials and workers before construction began, though there the temple stood finished before its dedication, while here the community worships at length on bare ground. The phrase 'as one man' in verse 1 borrows an idiom used at Israel's most solemn covenant assemblies, when the tribes mobilized against Gibeah and when the returned exiles later gathered to hear the Law read, to signal that this is a covenant gathering, not a mere crowd. The third movement turns from narration to song: verse 11 preserves the actual antiphonal refrain the priests and Levites sang, set responsively as David king of Israel had prescribed, before the narrative voice returns to record the crowd's uncontainable, mingled noise. That final image, an indistinguishable roar of joy and grief heard from far off, is left deliberately unresolved, a literary open question the book does not answer until the prophets Haggai and Zechariah are introduced two chapters later.
context.historical: The seventh month is Tishrei, the axis of Israel's ritual calendar: the Feast of Trumpets falls on its first day, the Day of Atonement on its tenth, and the Feast of Tabernacles from its fifteenth through its twenty first day, so the returning families restarted the sacrificial system during the single busiest fortnight of worship in the whole year. Cedar shipped from Lebanon through the ports of Sidon and Tyre by sea to Joppa, verse 7, repeats almost word for word the arrangement Solomon made with Hiram of Tyre for the first temple, a deliberate echo that let the builders and their audience measure the modest new project against the glorious original. The people of the land who made the remnant afraid were the mixed populations settled in Samaria and the surrounding regions after the Assyrian deportations of the eighth century, together with Ammonite, Moabite, Edomite, and Arab neighbors who had profited from Judah's long emptiness and had no wish to see a fortified, worshiping community reestablished on their border. The many elderly priests, Levites, and family heads who wept had likely been children or young men when Nebuchadnezzar's army burned Solomon's temple in 586 BC, so their tears in roughly 536 BC came from living memory, not legend, a gap of about fifty years that Haggai will later address directly.
context.canonical: The refrain the priests and Levites sing in verse 11, for he is good, for his loving devotion to Israel endures forever, is not new composition; it is drawn from the liturgy David established when the ark was first brought to Jerusalem and it became Israel's standard song of thanksgiving, repeated at Solomon's dedication and gathered into Psalm 136. By having the sons of Asaph lead it as David king of Israel had prescribed, verse 10, the narrator ties this ragged, half built assembly to the full flowering of Davidic worship, insisting that the small remnant stands in unbroken continuity with the glory of the united kingdom. The mixed shout of joy and weeping that closes the chapter is picked up directly two chapters later, when Haggai confronts the survivors who saw the former house in its former glory and asks whether the present house looks like nothing in their eyes, then answers with a promise that the latter glory will exceed the former, a word later echoed in Zechariah's rebuke of those who despise the day of small things. The tension is only fully resolved at the far end of the canon, where the tears of an unfinished, threatened people give way to the promise that God himself will wipe away every tear from his people's eyes forever.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Ezra wrote for a community that could easily read its own smallness as failure, a few thousand returnees, a modest budget, hostile neighbors, and a building site that for months held nothing but an altar. His intent is to reframe that smallness as faithfulness. By stressing four times in six verses that the people acted as it is written and in accordance with what is written, he wants his first readers, likely tempted by their own generation to cut corners or delay further, to see that obedience to the revealed pattern of worship, not the size of the building, is what makes a restoration real. He also wants them to hold two true things together without flattening either, that genuine fear of enemies is compatible with genuine obedience, verse 3, and that grief over diminished glory is compatible with genuine praise, verses 12 to 13. The chapter teaches its readers to keep building, and keep worshiping, even when the emotional and material evidence is mixed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Nothing here commands New Testament believers to reinstitute burnt offerings, New Moon sacrifices, or the Feast of Tabernacles as sacrifices, those forms belonged to a system that could never take away sins and that Christ has fulfilled and closed. What the passage does teach by example rather than command is a set of postures, gathering as one man rather than drifting apart into private practice, restoring right worship before securing personal comfort, following a received pattern rather than improvising one's own, and building even while still exposed and afraid rather than waiting for safety first. The elders' choice to keep the twice daily offerings and the appointed feasts before the temple existed also models a principle that outlasts the ceremonial law itself, the rhythm of daily and seasonal worship should not wait on ideal circumstances.

debates.question: Why did the older men weep when the foundation was laid?

views.label: Grief at a lesser glory
views.case: Those who remembered Solomon's magnificent temple saw how modest this one would be; Haggai 2:3 confirms the comparison, so their weeping expressed genuine sorrow that the restored house could not match the former glory.

views.label: Mixed sorrow and repentant memory
views.case: Their tears also recalled the sin and judgment that had destroyed the first temple; the weeping mingled loss, humility, and a chastened awareness of how far the nation had fallen, even as others rejoiced at God's mercy in beginning again.

debates.bearing: Both readings set up the prophetic answer: God would not leave His people to mourn a small beginning, but promised in Haggai 2:9 to fill the latter house with greater glory, fulfilled in the coming of Christ.

debates.question: Why rebuild the altar before the temple?

views.label: Atonement and worship come first
views.case: The people could not wait for a finished building to draw near to God; they needed the altar's sacrifices for atonement and daily fellowship at once, showing that right worship, not architecture, is the heart of restoration.

views.label: Obedience to the written pattern
views.case: The Law centered Israel's life on sacrifice at the appointed place, so restoring the altar and the feasts as it is written was the obedient way to re-establish covenant life, even before the temple structure rose.

debates.bearing: Either way, the priority is clear: God's people begin their renewal at the altar, in atoning, obedient worship, a priority answered finally at the cross.

study.originalLanguages: Beyond the altar, the burnt offering, and the covenant word already named in the basic reading, four more words carry the weight of this chapter. The assembly of verse 1 comes as one man, ke'ish echad, an idiom used elsewhere only for Israel's most solemn covenant gatherings, when the tribes mobilized against Gibeah, Judges 20:1, and when the returned exiles later gathered to hear the Law read, Nehemiah 8:1; Ezra reaches for the same phrase to signal that this is not a crowd drifting together but a covenant nation reconstituting itself. The word for the temple's foundation, repeated four times in verses 6, 10, 11, and 12, is yesod, a noun built on a verb meaning to found or establish; it is deliberately distinct from the word for the altar's own base in verse 3, mekonah, a fixed site or stand, so that the chapter can track two separate foundings, first of the altar's standing place, months later of the house itself, and can build toward the single dramatic moment when yesod finally appears with the weight of an accomplished act. The great shout the people raise in verse 11, teruah, is not a generic cheer; it is the same technical term used for the ritual trumpet blast that opens the Feast of Trumpets on the first day of this very month, Numbers 29:1, Leviticus 23:24, so that the shout at the foundation deliberately echoes, only weeks later, the blast that had opened Israel's sacred new year. The singing itself is described with the verb anah, to answer or respond, the standard term for antiphonal song sung in alternating parts, matching the responsive form of the refrain quoted in verse 11. And running underneath all of it is the verb yare, to fear, used once of the people's fear of their hostile neighbors, verse 3, and, throughout the wider Old Testament, of the fear of the LORD that is the beginning of wisdom, Proverbs 9:10; the narrator lets the same root describe a fear that could have silenced worship and a fear that in fact never displaced it, since the sacrifices went up regardless. Taken together these five words trace a single movement, a covenant people gathering as one, founding a house, fearing yet obeying, and answering with a shout that borrows the very sound of Israel's sacred calendar.

typology.type: The altar rebuilt before the temple
typology.fulfillment: The remnant established the place of sacrifice months before the building around it existed, showing that atonement, not architecture, is the true foundation of fellowship with God. Hebrews draws out what this could only picture: the blood of bulls and goats offered morning and evening can never take away sins, Hebrews 10:4, 11, so every fresh sacrifice testified to its own insufficiency even as it pointed forward. Christ's single offering does what the altar's endless repetition could not, dealing with sin once for all, Hebrews 10:12, 14, so that no rebuilt altar has been needed since.

typology.type: The foundation and the finished house
typology.fulfillment: Laying the yesod, the foundation, was treated as an event worth its own liturgy, because everything the finished temple would become depended on what was set down first. Paul makes the same logic explicit for the church: no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ, 1 Corinthians 3:11, and apostles and prophets themselves are merely built on that one foundation stone, with Christ as the chief cornerstone, Ephesians 2:20, the very language Isaiah had used centuries earlier of a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion, Isaiah 28:16. The remnant's small, wept over foundation was never the true and final one; it only ever pointed toward it.

Restoring the Feast of Tabernacles, which remembered Israel dwelling in temporary shelters in the wilderness under God's daily provision, celebrated a God who pitches his tent among a homeless, exposed people. John reaches for the very same word when he writes that the Word became flesh and dwelt, literally tabernacled, among us, John 1:14, and Revelation completes the picture with the loud voice declaring that the dwelling place of God is with man forever, Revelation 21:3. The feast the remnant kept in fear under threat becomes, in Christ, an unshakeable and permanent dwelling.

study.christ: The chapter's most quietly messianic thread runs through Zerubbabel himself. Zechariah, prophesying to this very generation, twice names the Branch as the one who will build the temple of the LORD, Zechariah 6:12 to 13, and promises that the hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house, his hands will also complete it, Zechariah 4:9, language that reaches past the governor to a greater son of David who alone finishes what he starts. When Jesus later stands in the courts of this very building, rebuilt again by Herod, and declares that something greater than the temple is here, Matthew 12:6, he is claiming the reality that every foundation laid in Ezra 3 could only anticipate, God himself present among his people, not housed by a structure but embodied in a person. The people gathered as one man before they built anything, a covenant unity around worship that Paul says Christ achieves permanently, killing the hostility between former strangers and creating in himself one new man in place of the two, Ephesians 2:14 to 15, so that the church, not a rebuilt courtyard, becomes the true assembly gathered as one. The mixed cry of joy and weeping also anticipates something the sacrifices themselves could never resolve. Every burnt offering that went up morning and evening was a fresh reminder of sin still unpaid, which is exactly why the offerings could never take away sins, Hebrews 10:11, even while being offered in faith. The tears of verse 12 are, in that light, more than nostalgia for lost architecture; they are the grief of people still waiting for an atonement large enough to end the waiting. Christ answers both threads at once. As the true Branch he builds a house not made with hands, and as the final sacrifice he ends the cycle the returned exiles had only just restarted, so that the weeping of Ezra 3 gives way, in him, to a joy no shout of trumpets could ever fully picture.
study.god: The God of this chapter is worshiped before he is housed, which says something important about who he is, he does not wait behind a finished building for acceptable conditions before receiving his people's praise, and the elders do not treat his presence as contingent on complete architecture. That is consistent with the confession that would later be made in Solomon's own dedicated temple, that heaven itself cannot contain him, 1 Kings 8:27, and, further on, that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands, Acts 7:48. He is also a God who has bound his own character to a fixed liturgical formula, the refrain the priests sing in verse 11, and its two clauses are not decorative; good describes what he is in himself, and loving devotion describes what he does for his covenant people, so that the song joins his nature to his fidelity in a single breath, exactly the pairing Israel had sung since David first brought the ark to Jerusalem. He is patient with imperfect worship. The people build the altar even though they feared the people of the land, verse 3, and God does not demand that fear be resolved into confidence before he accepts their sacrifices, obedient worship offered in the middle of real fear is still received. And he is large enough to hold together responses that human worship leaders would be tempted to smooth into one mood. The text insists twice that the sound could not be told apart, joy from grief, and never resolves which is the truer response, both the shout and the weeping rise to the same LORD, and both are, in their way, forms of faith, one confident in what God has begun, the other honest about what has been lost. A God who can receive both without demanding uniformity is a God who deals gently with his people's mixed and unfinished hearts.

crossReferences.note: Just months after the foundation is laid with joy and weeping, Haggai confronts the very people who remembered Solomon's temple and asks whether this house looks like nothing beside it, then promises that its latter glory will surpass the former, a word aimed directly at Ezra 3's mixed tears.

Zechariah promises that the same hands which laid this foundation, Zerubbabel's, will also finish the house, and rebukes anyone who despises the day of small things, answering in advance the grief of the older generation who wept at how modest the new foundation looked.

The prophet names a coming figure called the Branch who will build the temple of the LORD and rule as priest and king together, reaching past Zerubbabel toward a greater builder whose house this remnant's small beginning only anticipates.

Israel's tribes gathered as one man to confront Gibeah's sin, the same rare idiom Ezra uses for the returned exiles assembling in Jerusalem, marking their gathering as a solemn, covenant shaped assembly rather than a casual crowd.

At the dedication of the first temple Solomon confesses that the heavens, even the highest heaven, cannot contain God, a truth that already relativizes any building, however small or grand, that this later, humbler foundation would raise.

The Law names the first day of the seventh month a day of trumpet blast, the very word used for the people's great shout at the foundation, tying their worship back to the sacred new year they had just begun keeping.

When David first brought the ark to Jerusalem he appointed this exact refrain, give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, his loving devotion endures forever, making the returned exiles' song at the foundation a deliberate echo of Israel's oldest worship.

Paul describes the church as a household built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ himself as the cornerstone, growing into a holy temple in the Lord, the reality toward which every stone laid in Ezra 3 was pointing.

The writer contrasts the priest who stands daily offering the same sacrifices that can never take away sins with Christ, who offered one sacrifice for sins forever and sat down, showing exactly why the endless burnt offerings of Ezra 3 could only foreshadow, never finish, atonement.

Paul insists that no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, Jesus Christ, so that the modest foundation celebrated in verse 11 stands as a picture of, but never a substitute for, the one foundation on which God's true house is built.

study.oneStory: Genesis ends its opening scenes with God walking among his creatures in a garden; by the time Israel's history reaches Ezra 3, that nearness has been lost twice over, first at Eden's gate and then, more recently, when the glory departed a corrupted temple and the building itself was burned to the ground. Ezra 3 sits at the point where a scattered people begin, tentatively, to reclaim the pattern God gave at Sinai, an altar first, because access to a holy God has always run through sacrifice, then a house, because he intends to dwell among his people, not merely forgive them from a distance. The chapter's honesty matters for the shape of the whole story. It refuses to pretend that a partial recovery feels like unmixed victory; the same crowd that shouts also weeps, because true restoration this side of Christ is always real but incomplete, a foundation and not yet a finished house. That incompleteness becomes the very hinge the prophets use to keep Israel looking forward rather than settling for what has been rebuilt, Haggai will promise a latter glory greater than Solomon's, and Zechariah will point past Zerubbabel to a coming Branch who builds and reigns at once. The whole trajectory comes to rest in Jesus, who is himself both the true altar, where the last sacrifice was finally offered, and the true temple, in whom God dwells among his people bodily and permanently. What Ezra 3 could only inaugurate with fear and tears, the New Testament announces as accomplished and secure, and what still lies ahead, God's dwelling filling not one city but the whole renewed creation, Revelation pictures as a joy with no more weeping mixed into it, Revelation 21:3 to 4. The remnant's mingled shout is a way station on the road from Eden lost to Eden restored, and Christ is the one who walks that whole road for his people.

quiz.q: What did the returned exiles build first, before the temple itself?

options.text: The altar, so they could restore the sacrifices and worship God at once.
options.note: Verses 2-3 show the altar rebuilt first, prioritizing atoning worship.

options.text: The city walls, for protection against their enemies.
options.note: The walls come much later, in Nehemiah; here the priority is the altar.

options.text: Their own houses and marketplaces.
options.note: Personal housing is not the focus here; worship of God comes first.

options.text: A palace for Zerubbabel.
options.note: No palace is built; the concern is the worship of God.

quiz.q: What phrase repeatedly describes how they carried out their worship?

options.text: As it is written, or in accordance with what is written, following the Law of Moses.
options.note: The chapter stresses obedience to God's revealed word in worship.

options.text: As seemed best to the leaders at the time.
options.note: The opposite: they deliberately followed the written pattern, not their own judgment.

options.text: As the surrounding nations worshiped their gods.
options.note: They distanced themselves from the peoples of the land, worshiping as God commanded.

options.text: In secret, so no one would notice.
options.note: Their worship was public and their praise was heard from afar.

quiz.q: Why was the sound at the laying of the foundation so confusing?

options.text: Shouts of joy and loud weeping mixed together and could not be told apart.
options.note: Verses 12-13 describe joy and grief blending into one great sound.

options.text: The trumpets drowned out the singing entirely.
options.note: The instruments were part of it, but the confusion was joy mixed with weeping.

options.text: The people were arguing about how to build.
options.note: It was worship, not argument, that filled the air.

options.text: An enemy attack interrupted the ceremony.
options.note: No attack occurs here; the mingled sound was joy and weeping.

quiz.q: Why did many of the older men weep at the foundation?

options.text: They had seen Solomon's temple and grieved that this one seemed so much smaller.
options.note: Verse 12 and Haggai 2:3 point to sorrow over the lesser glory.

options.text: They did not believe God had brought them home.
options.note: They did believe; their grief was over the diminished temple, not unbelief.

options.text: They were angry at Zerubbabel's leadership.
options.note: The text names sorrow over the former temple, not anger at leaders.

options.text: They wanted to return to Babylon.
options.note: Nothing suggests a wish to return; they wept over the smaller house.

quiz.q: How does the altar-first priority point to Christ?

options.text: It shows that fellowship with God rests on sacrifice, fulfilled once for all in Christ, our true altar and Lamb.
options.note: The sacrifices foreshadow Christ's final, atoning offering.

options.text: It teaches that we must still offer animal sacrifices today.
options.note: Christ has fulfilled and ended the sacrifices; we do not repeat them.

options.text: It proves buildings matter more than worship.
options.note: The point is the reverse: worship and atonement come before the building.

options.text: It has nothing to do with Christ.
options.note: The altar and sacrifices point directly to Christ's atoning work.

questions: The remnant made worship of God their very first priority, even before securing their own comfort. What does the order of your priorities reveal about where God sits in your life?
They worshiped as it is written, shaping their approach to God by His word rather than their own ideas. Where might you be tempted to worship God on your own terms instead of His?
They rebuilt the altar even though they feared the hostile peoples around them. Where is fear tempting you to hold back from obeying God, and what would faithful obedience look like anyway?
The same event brought some to tears and others to shouts of joy. How do you hold honest grief and real thanksgiving together in a season that is both hard and hopeful?
God promised to fill the latter temple with greater glory, fulfilled in Christ. How does knowing that your best days are secured in Jesus reshape the way you face small and disappointing beginnings?

translationNotes.note: The clause both the morning and evening burnt offerings specifies the twice-daily offerings prescribed in the Law.
Loving devotion renders the Hebrew chesed; the BSB footnote notes its range, love, goodness, kindness, faithfulness, mercy, and covenant loyalty. The refrain echoes Psalm 136 and 1 Chronicles 16:34.
Those who had seen the first temple were elderly, since some fifty years had passed since its destruction; their comparison is the concern Haggai later addresses directly.
